projects.title: Build a lunar expedition
projects.brief: Pack the supplies, feel their effect on a rocket, and choose a safe mathematical orbit.
projects.assumptions: An original classroom scenario: full 5 L water tanks each weigh 2 kg empty; water is modeled at 1 kg/L. The vehicle without these tanks has dry mass 2000 kg. The rocket burn is ideal deep-space motion. The lunar orbit is a separate two-body scenario, not a computed Earth-to-Moon trajectory.

stages.title: Give the crew enough water
stages.challenge: Choose a crew and stay length. Pack full tanks and compare needed water with the water actually carried.
stages.prediction: Before moving a control, predict what doubling the stay does to the water and tank count.
stages.decision: Record your crew, days and tanks. Explain why rounding down could fail.
stages.connection: Your full water tanks become payload in the next stage. Their extra capacity has mass too.

stages.title: Feel the payload penalty
stages.challenge: The dry mass now includes your packed water and tank shells. Keep propellant fixed and return to the first stage to try a longer stay.
stages.prediction: Will the same propellant give a heavier vehicle more or less ideal velocity gain? Explain before testing.
stages.decision: Compare two supply plans. Record their dry masses and ideal velocity gains; choose a plan and explain the tradeoff.
stages.connection: dry mass = 2000 + (5 + 2) × tank count, in kilograms. Supplies flow into this model automatically.

stages.title: Choose how the burn unfolds
stages.challenge: Keep your payload and propellant. Compare halfway through the burn with just before fuel exhaustion. Then change the mass flow.
stages.prediction: How should acceleration change as fuel leaves the rocket? Does changing flow change the ideal total velocity gain when mass ratio stays fixed?
stages.decision: Use two nearby times to estimate acceleration. Compare your estimate with the model readout and explain the units.
stages.connection: You are differentiating the velocity of the design you already chose. At cutoff, powered acceleration ends.

stages.title: Turn a speed curve into distance
stages.challenge: Use your saved burn design. Estimate distance from a few rectangles under its velocity curve, then compare the exact model distance.
stages.prediction: For this increasing velocity curve, will left-endpoint rectangles underestimate or overestimate distance?
stages.decision: Show your time widths and speeds. Explain how refining the rectangles changes the approximation.
stages.connection: The derivative explains acceleration; the integral explains distance for the same saved burn.

stages.title: Find a lunar orbit that clears the surface
stages.challenge: In a separate lunar scenario, select Circular, then Ellipse. Change tangential speed and inspect the closest approach to the surface.
stages.prediction: Does a closed mathematical ellipse always keep a spacecraft above the Moon?
stages.decision: Choose a starting altitude and speed that avoid surface contact. Record closest/farthest altitude and justify your choice.
stages.connection: The rocket and orbit panels illustrate different phases under different assumptions. This app does not calculate the transfer between them.

stages.title: Defend the whole design
stages.challenge: Use the same orbit. Compare equal time intervals near the closest and farthest points, then write a final mission brief using the saved supply and burn decisions.
stages.prediction: Will equal time intervals correspond to equal distances around the ellipse?
stages.decision: Explain your supplies, payload cost, burn behavior and orbital geometry. Identify two omitted effects a real mission would need.
stages.connection: One project now links arithmetic, algebra, geometry, rates and accumulation. Your argument awaits review; a working model is not proof of full understanding.

projects.title: Build a tiny game world
projects.brief: Transform a player sprite, make a reversible camera, then deliver its movement over a network.
projects.assumptions: The sprite lives in a flat 2D world. Transformations scale, rotate, then translate. Network delays and independent per-edge failures are invented teaching quantities.

stages.title: Place the player
stages.challenge: Set scale factors to 1 and rotation to 0. Move the player horizontally and track two vertices.
stages.prediction: Will translation change distances between vertices?
stages.decision: Write two before/after coordinate pairs and explain the common change.
stages.connection: Keep this sprite placement as the starting design for the next stage.

stages.title: Turn and stretch the sprite
stages.challenge: Keep the saved translation. Rotate 90 degrees and compare uniform with unequal scaling.
stages.prediction: Which changes preserve the sprite's shape? What happens to a direction vector after a quarter turn?
stages.decision: Use the matrix and transformed points to explain your chosen appearance.
stages.connection: Your coordinate rules become the columns of a transformation matrix.

stages.title: Make the camera reversible
stages.challenge: Try a zero scale factor, then a negative one. Inspect the determinant and image.
stages.prediction: Which design destroys information needed to recover the original point?
stages.decision: Choose a reversible transformation. Explain what the sign and size of its determinant say about the picture.
stages.connection: A camera must translate a click back into the game world; an information-destroying map cannot always do that.

stages.title: Keep multiplayer movement responsive
stages.challenge: Choose route delays, then compare the fastest route with alternatives that use fewer edges.
stages.prediction: Must the fastest route also deliver the highest expected fraction of packets?
stages.decision: Use latency and delivery probability to justify a networking choice for your game.
stages.connection: Your final design joins coordinate geometry, matrix structure and a graph-based communication decision.

projects.title: Design a sound signature
projects.brief: Build a tone, add a harmonic, explore cancellation and explain the energy of your final sound.
projects.assumptions: Two ideal sine waves are added linearly. The display uses relative amplitude and a quiet synthetic preview. RMS is a mathematical signal measure, not a complete model of perceived loudness.

stages.title: Choose the repeating pattern
stages.challenge: Set the second amplitude to zero. Pick a base frequency and use the table to follow time to output.
stages.prediction: What happens to the period if you double the frequency?
stages.decision: Record frequency and period. Explain their reciprocal relationship with units.
stages.connection: Your frequency stays with the project as you build a richer waveform.

stages.title: Add another repeating pattern
stages.challenge: Increase the second amplitude and try harmonic 2, then 3, keeping your base tone.
stages.prediction: Will the combined waveform still repeat after one base period?
stages.decision: Describe which parts of the wave changed. Explain how two functions produce the displayed sum.
stages.connection: Both components share a common repeating interval because the second frequency is an integer multiple.

stages.title: Create and explain a silent setting
stages.challenge: Use harmonic 1 and equal amplitudes. Compare phase 0 with phase 180 degrees.
stages.prediction: Can two nonzero waves add to zero at every time? State the conditions.
stages.decision: Explain the cancellation using a sine identity, then show why changing one amplitude breaks it.
stages.connection: Keep the distinction between equal frequency cancellation and two different harmonics.

stages.title: Choose a final waveform and justify it
stages.challenge: Choose a non-silent final sound. Compare peak shape with the displayed RMS and inspect values across a full period.
stages.prediction: Does the average signed wave height measure its strength well?
stages.decision: Explain why squaring, averaging and taking a root gives a useful signal measure. Defend your design and state what the model cannot say about real listeners.
stages.connection: Your saved tone now connects functions, trigonometry, superposition and integration.

projects.title: Keep a solar-powered event running
projects.brief: Budget energy through a whole day, size storage and investigate why enough daily energy may still leave a blackout.
projects.assumptions: Synthetic solar power follows a sine curve between 06:00 and 18:00. Load is constant, efficiency is ideal, the battery starts half full, and dispatch uses half-minute intervals. This is an invented planning exercise.

stages.title: Budget the daily demand
stages.challenge: Choose a constant load. Convert that power to a 24-hour energy demand before inspecting the readout.
stages.prediction: If the load doubles, how does daily demand change?
stages.decision: Write the multiplication with units and compare two event sizes.
stages.connection: The selected load persists as you design generation and storage.

stages.title: Size the solar array
stages.challenge: Keep your load and change peak solar power. Compare daily production with demand.
stages.prediction: Is peak power times 12 hours the actual area under this curved production graph?
stages.decision: Estimate or integrate the area and state a necessary energy-budget condition for your design.
stages.connection: An energy total is useful, but it does not say when that energy arrives.

stages.title: Carry energy through the night
stages.challenge: Keep production above daily demand, then try a very small battery. Increase capacity and watch unmet demand and spilled energy.
stages.prediction: Can a positive daily energy surplus coexist with unmet demand?
stages.decision: Find a feasible design within the controls or explain why your target is infeasible. Identify when storage becomes the limiting constraint.
stages.connection: Your earlier energy budget now meets a time-dependent storage constraint.

stages.title: Choose between two feasible designs
stages.challenge: Compare two combinations that meet your demand. For an invented budget, use cost = 800 × peak kW + 200 × battery kWh.
stages.prediction: Will increasing solar production always be the cheapest way to remove an energy shortage?
stages.decision: Compute both costs, compare service and explain your choice. State why comparing two designs does not prove a global optimum.
stages.connection: The final decision combines ratios, accumulation, constraints and optimization with explicit modeling limits.
